questions.q: You run `mkdir app/logs` and get "No such file or directory", even though you want logs to live inside app. What's the fix?
options: Run `mkdir -p app/logs` to create any missing parent directories
Run `touch app/logs` instead
Run `mkdir app` and `mkdir logs` in the same directory
mkdir cannot create subdirectories under any circumstances
questions.explain: Plain mkdir only creates one level at a time. The -p flag tells mkdir to create every missing directory in the path, including app itself if it doesn't exist yet.

questions.q: Why does `cp app_backup app` fail with "omitting directory" when app_backup is a directory?
options: cp cannot copy to a destination that already exists
The directory name is too long
Plain cp refuses to copy directories unless you add the -r (recursive) flag
cp only works on files ending in .txt
questions.explain: cp only copies individual files by default. Copying a directory and its contents requires the -r flag, which tells cp to recurse into the directory.

questions.q: Why is `mv` used for both renaming a file and moving it to another directory?
options: Linux has two separate rename and move commands that happen to share a name
Renaming and moving are the same underlying operation — changing where a filename points
mv only renames files; moving requires cp followed by rm
mv requires the -r flag to rename a file
questions.explain: There is no separate 'rename' command in Linux because renaming in place and moving to a new location are the same operation: pointing a name at a new location, whether that location is in the same directory or a different one.

questions.q: Why doesn't `mv` require a -r flag to move a directory, while `cp` does require -r to copy one?
options: mv is simply a newer, more modern command than cp
Moving a directory just changes its location pointer, without needing to duplicate every file inside it the way a copy does
mv actually does require -r, and the question is a trick
Directories cannot be moved on Linux, only renamed
questions.explain: A copy must physically duplicate every file inside a directory, which is why cp needs -r to recurse. A move just changes where the directory's name points, so there's nothing recursive to do.

questions.q: What is the main danger of running `rm -rf` as root?
options: It only works on empty directories
It asks for confirmation before every file, which can be accidentally dismissed
It permanently deletes files and directories with no confirmation and no Recycle Bin to recover from, so a typo in the path can be catastrophic
It automatically backs up deleted files to /tmp before removing them
questions.explain: rm -rf deletes recursively, forces past confirmation prompts, and leaves no undo. A stray space in the path (e.g. '/ app_backup/' instead of '/app_backup/') can delete far more than intended.
